summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived article on Guam, covering its political status, geography, tourism economy, and ecology. It also describes the Chamorro people's wartime treatment under Japanese occupation and post-war resentment with the Northern Marianas Chamorros, the 2007 coconut rhinoceros beetle infestation, the loss of native birds to the brown tree snake, and the blend of influences in Chamorro culture. The main points are Guam's status as an unincorporated US territory and the environmental and cultural effects of colonial contact.
one_line: Overview of Guam, a US territory in the western Pacific, covering its status, tourism, invasive species, native birds, and Chamorro culture.
key_facts: Guam is an unincorporated and organized territory of the United States located in the northwestern Pacific Ocean.
The capital city of Guam is Hagåtña, and the most populous city is Dededo.
Guam has an area of 544 km2 (210 sq mi), and it is the largest and southernmost of the Mariana Islands.
The highest point on Guam is Mount Lamlam at 406 meters (1,332 ft) above sea level.
The coconut rhinoceros beetle infestation was detected on Guam on September 12, 2007, and was limited to Tumon Bay and Faifai Beach.
The Guam Organic Act of 1950 established Guam as an unincorporated organized territory and granted the people U.S. citizenship.
The Governor of Guam was federally appointed until 1968, when the Guam Elective Governor Act provided for the office's popular election.
The brown tree snake (Boiga irregularis) was accidentally introduced to Guam near the end of World War II, and it nearly eliminated the native bird population.
As many as twelve bird species are believed to have been driven to extinction by the brown tree snake on Guam.
The Guam flycatcher is entirely extinct, while the Guam rail is extinct in the wild but bred in captivity by the Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources.
Tumon, the tourist hub, features over 20 large hotels, and the island's hotels and seven public golf courses accommodate over a million tourists per year.
About 75% of Guam's tourists are Japanese, and the island also receives tourists from South Korea, the U.S., the Philippines, and Taiwan.
During Spanish colonial rule (1668–1898), the majority of the population was converted to Roman Catholicism.
Under Japanese occupation, the Guamanian Chamorros were treated as an occupied enemy, which caused lasting resentment toward the Chamorros of the Northern Marianas.
